metadata.purpose: Pretest taken before day 1. An instructor reads one day's items to set each student's entry to that day's lab.
metadata.lab_entry_rule: A student who gets every item for a day right is offered that day's problem; everyone else starts at the worked example. There is no overall cut score.
metadata.blueprint: docs/build-spec.md, Pretest blueprint (concept numbers are the Role Concepts Order, as of 30 Oct 2026)
metadata.grading: Multiple-choice items score right or wrong. A written item is right when the answer states every point in its answer_key, in any wording.
metadata.post_test: Each item has a post_test note: the parallel item tests the same concept at the same skill level through a new scenario.

lectures.title: Day 5: VASPs, the rules and permissioned ledgers

questions.question_stem: A wallet signs two payments that spend the same coins, one to Carol and one to Dave. Each payment is valid on its own. What decides which one the ledger keeps?
questions.correct_answer: Consensus: the network's rule for agreeing on one history picks one, and every honest node then accepts it.
incorrect_answers: The signatures: only one of the two can carry a valid signature, so every node simply rejects the other one.
The timestamps: each node keeps the payment the wallet signed first and drops the later one for good.
The hashes: the payment whose hash is lower wins, so every node can work out the result on its own.
questions.explanation: Both payments carry valid signatures and hashes, so neither can choose between them. Different nodes may see a different one first; consensus is what makes every honest node accept the same history.

questions.question_stem: An Ethereum explorer shows an address holding 3 ETH. A Bitcoin wallet shows its owner holding 3 BTC. Where does each figure come from?
questions.correct_answer: The ETH figure is read from the account's stored balance; the BTC figure is added up from unspent outputs the keys can spend.
incorrect_answers: Both are read from a balance field that each chain stores for every address and updates with each newly mined block.
The BTC figure is read from a stored balance; the ETH figure is added up from unspent outputs held by the address.
Both are added up by the wallet or explorer, because neither chain stores a balance for any single address or account.
questions.explanation: Bitcoin stores unspent outputs, not balances: a wallet or explorer adds them up. Ethereum stores accounts with an address, balance and nonce, so the balance is read from the account.
questions.lesson_block: Bitcoin keeps no balances, only unspent coins

questions.question_stem: A suspect claims the recipient address in a signed transaction was changed after they signed it. What does the signature let an analyst check?
questions.correct_answer: Whether these exact bytes were signed: change one byte and the signature no longer verifies against the key.
incorrect_answers: Who signed it: a valid signature names the person who held the private key at the moment the transaction was approved.
Nothing about the recipient: a signature covers the amount and fee but leaves the addresses unprotected.
When it was signed: the signature carries a timestamp that shows whether the address was edited later.
questions.explanation: A valid signature proves that someone with the private key approved this exact transaction. Any changed byte, the recipient included, makes it fail to verify. It shows a key, not a person.
questions.lesson_block: A signature binds the key to these exact bytes

specific_source.reading: A signature binds the key to these exact bytes

sources.slide: A signature binds the key to these exact bytes
A signature authorizes; it doesn't identify

questions.post_test: Same concept, new claim: the amount was raised after signing; or ask what a hash, rather than a signature, lets the analyst check.

questions.question_stem: Your node lists a transaction as unconfirmed. A colleague's explorer has no record of it at all. What best explains the difference?
questions.correct_answer: Each node keeps its own mempool; one can hold a payment another never saw or dropped.
incorrect_answers: Explorers hide unconfirmed payments until a miner has placed them in a block on the chain.
Your node is out of step with the one shared mempool that all nodes on the network read.
The payment was censored, so it was struck from the single global mempool for every node.
questions.explanation: There is no single mempool: each full node keeps its own list of unconfirmed transactions, so any node's or explorer's view is one among many. Censorship is one explanation to rule out, not the default.

questions.post_test: Same concept, new case: a low-fee transaction has sat unconfirmed for a day; ask which explanations stay open.

questions.question_stem: Monitoring shows that node N was the first to relay a Bitcoin payment to its peers. What can an analyst say about who sent the payment?
questions.correct_answer: Low confidence that N's operator sent it: many wallets broadcast through someone else's node, not their own.
incorrect_answers: High confidence that N's operator sent it: a payment can enter the network only through its sender's own node.
Nothing at all: every payment passes through a central server first, so relay order is never recorded.
Moderate confidence that N mined it: the first node to relay a payment is the miner who will confirm it.
questions.explanation: Nodes check and relay payments peer to peer, with no central server. Researchers have linked payments to IP addresses by watching which node relayed first, but on its own that is Low: wallets often send through other people's nodes.

questions.post_test: Same concept, new question: ask what each node checks before relaying, or why there is no central server that holds relay records.

questions.question_stem: A Bitcoin explorer page for one transaction shows: the txid; "Block 840,100"; two outputs, each with an amount and an address; the input amount; the fee; and a tag reading "Exchange" on one output address. The explorer's latest block is 840,105. (a) Sort the items on the page into three groups: read from the chain, worked out by the explorer, and added by the explorer's operator. (b) How many confirmations does the transaction have? (c) What weight does the "Exchange" tag carry in your assessment?
answer_key: From the chain: the txid, the block, and the outputs (amounts and addresses).
Worked out: the input amount and the fee (inputs minus outputs), computed from earlier transactions.
Added by the operator: the "Exchange" tag.
Confirmations: 840,105 - 840,100 + 1 = 6, true only at the moment it is read.
The tag is Low confidence on its own: a lead to check, not a fact.
questions.explanation: An explorer shows what a node holds, plus figures it works out and labels it adds. Rely on the chain data and check the rest. Confirmations count the payment's own block and every block on top.
questions.lesson_block: An explorer is a node's record, plus extras

specific_source.reading: An explorer is a node's record, plus extras

sources.slide: An explorer is a node's record, plus extras
Each block on top adds one confirmation

questions.question_stem: During a live case, why might an analyst look up a suspect's address on a node they run rather than on a public block explorer?
questions.correct_answer: A public explorer sees each address looked up and the IP address it came from; one's own node does not.
incorrect_answers: Only one's own node holds the real chain; a public explorer shows a copy that its operator may edit.
A public explorer cannot show balances; only a node queried directly can add up what an address currently holds.
Public explorers run hours behind the chain, so only one's own node shows the latest block in time.
questions.explanation: Looking at a live chain through someone else's service tells them what you are interested in. With your own node you are not sending your IP address or queries to a third party.
questions.lesson_block: Live data has costs, so we use captured data

specific_source.reading: Live data has costs, so we use captured data

sources.slide: Live data has costs, so we use captured data

questions.post_test: Same concept, other side: ask which page figures a node's own answer does not give (worked-out fee, operator tags).

answer_key: Create: no function creates tokens, so no one can mint more.
Move, holders: any holder can send their own tokens, up to their balance, only while the contract is not paused; each transfer emits Transfer.
Move, owner: only the owner's key can call seize, which moves tokens out of any address without that holder's signature; pausing does not stop it.
Limits: only the owner can pause or unpause transfers (setPaused).
Record: seize emits no event, so a tool that sums Transfer logs shows wrong balances after a seizure; read balances from the contract's state.
questions.explanation: The four questions (who can create, who can move, what limits, what is recorded) open any contract an analyst characterizes. Here the owner key controls every balance, and one of its moves leaves no Transfer log, as Tether's destroyBlackFunds does.

questions.question_stem: Stolen funds were swapped into 400,000 USDT on Ethereum and have sat at one address since block 21,000,000. The case agent asks what this means for the case. Write your answer to the agent, covering: (a) can the funds be frozen where they sit, by whom, and for how long; (b) what happens to USDT sent to the address after a freeze; (c) what your answer states about the holding and how sure you are (High, Moderate or Low); (d) who decides whether to ask for a freeze.
answer_key: Freezable in place: USDT has an issuer, Tether, whose key controls a blacklist in the token contract, so the address can be frozen.

Only while the funds stay in USDT: swapped into ETH or a token with no issuer they are out of reach; swapped into another stablecoin or bridged, the question goes to that issuer. The window is the time before the next move.
A frozen address can still receive USDT; it cannot send.
States the token, the amount, since which block, and a confidence word (High, Moderate or Low).
Leaves the freeze request to the agent: the analyst flags, the agent acts.
questions.explanation: A blacklist lives in one token's contract, so the funds are freezable only while they sit in that issuer's token. The analyst says what the address holds and how sure they are; asking the issuer is the agent's decision.

questions.question_stem: A user deposits ETH into a rollup's bridge contract on Ethereum, then makes 30 trades on the rollup. Where does the activity leave records?
questions.correct_answer: A deposit on Ethereum, the trades on the rollup, and batches of the trade data posted to Ethereum.
incorrect_answers: Only on the rollup: once the ETH is deposited, nothing about the user's trades ever goes back to Ethereum.
Only on Ethereum: a rollup is a contract, so each of the 30 trades is its own Ethereum transaction.
The deposit on Ethereum and the trades on the operator's private server, which posts nothing to Ethereum.
questions.explanation: A rollup executes transactions outside Ethereum, then posts the transaction data back to Ethereum as calldata or blobs. One user's activity shows up as an L1 deposit, many L2 transactions, and batches on L1.

questions.question_stem: 50 ETH goes into a bridge contract on Ethereum. Forty minutes later, 50 wrapped ETH is minted to a new address on another chain. (a) What kind of bridge is this, and what actually crossed? (b) How do you link the two sides? (c) Who could have stopped or frozen the funds? (d) Does wrapping hide the funds from a trace?
answer_key: Lock-and-mint: the ETH is locked in the bridge contract on Ethereum and a wrapped copy is minted on the other chain; a claim crossed, not the coin.
Link the lock and the mint by amount, time and the bridge's own event.
Wrapping does not hide the funds: the wrapped token is on a public ledger.
The bridge's operators can pause it; a token issuer can freeze its token on either side (none for ETH itself).
questions.explanation: A bridge moves a claim, not the coin. For lock-and-mint the evidence is the lock on chain A and the mint on chain B; the question to answer is who could have stopped it. By contrast, a liquidity or intents bridge pays from a relayer's own funds and usually no one can freeze.

questions.question_stem: A wallet sends 1,000,000 of token X into a Uniswap v2-style pool and receives 4 ETH, in one transaction sent to the Uniswap router. (a) Who was on the other side of the trade? (b) Which logs show the trade, and what do they tell you? (c) The wallet holds 50,000,000 more of token X. What do you check before calling this pool its exit, and could the pool itself freeze the funds?
answer_key: The other side was the pool contract, not a person: the trader swapped against its reserves, at a price its formula set.

Logs: Transfer logs show token X going into the pool and ETH (WETH) leaving it; the pool's Swap log shows the amounts in and out and the recipient (to); Sync shows the reserves after the trade. The router is only in the path: follow the output to whoever received it.

Before calling it an exit, at least: whether the pool is deep enough for 50,000,000 X (reserves from Sync or getReserves, and the price impact); who holds the LP tokens (they can withdraw the reserves); whether token X can be sold or frozen (its code and issuer).
The pool itself has no freeze.
questions.explanation: On a DEX the counterparty is code. A swap leaves token Transfer logs, a Swap log and a Sync log; the router only carries the trade. Whether a pool is an exit turns on its depth against the holding, who holds the LP tokens, and the token itself.

questions.question_stem: An exchange's records show that deposit address D belongs to an account verified in Jane Roe's name. Stolen funds were sent to D. What does this establish?
questions.correct_answer: The funds went into an account the exchange verified as Jane Roe's; who controlled that account still needs other evidence.
incorrect_answers: That Jane Roe sent the stolen funds herself, since an exchange verifies the person behind every incoming payment.
Nothing about anyone: exchanges keep no identity files for the deposit addresses they hand out to their own users.
That Jane Roe holds D's private key, since the exchange hands each verified customer the key to their deposit address.
questions.explanation: The deposit address an exchange assigns to a KYC'd account links to that file, and the exchange holds the deposit key. A KYC file names the account holder; it does not prove who controlled the account or sent the funds.

questions.question_stem: A FinCEN-registered exchange filed a Suspicious Activity Report (SAR) about a customer's transfers. How should the analyst treat the SAR?
questions.correct_answer: As a lead: the firm saw a pattern it judged suspicious, and the analyst still reads the chain themselves.
incorrect_answers: As a finding: FinCEN has already reviewed the transfers and confirmed that the customer laundered the funds.
As proof: a SAR is filed only after a court has found that the customer's activity was criminal.
As a record on chain: the SAR is written into the transfers so that every node can see the warning.
questions.explanation: Under the Bank Secrecy Act an MSB must file SARs where they apply. A SAR says a business saw something it judged suspicious: a lead, not a finding. The analyst still reads the chain.

questions.post_test: Same concept, other duty: ask what an exchange's retained records, rather than its reports, give the analyst.

questions.question_stem: Address A is not on OFAC's SDN list, but clustering puts it in the same wallet as a listed address. How should the analyst describe A?
questions.correct_answer: As a sanctions risk: a judgment carried with a confidence word, not a checkable fact like a listing.
incorrect_answers: As sanctioned outright: any address that clusters with a listed one is added to the SDN list as well.
As clear: only an address named in an SDN entry carries any sanctions risk for those who deal with it.
As proof of a violation: any exposure to a listed wallet shows that a sanctions offence has taken place.
questions.explanation: A listed address is a fact you can check. An address that shares a wallet with a listed one may pose sanctions risk, but linking it is a clustering judgment, so it carries a confidence word. Exposure is a risk signal, not proof.

questions.question_stem: A U.S. exchange sends $5,000 in USDC to another exchange for one of its customers. Where does the Travel Rule information about the sender go?
questions.correct_answer: From the sending exchange to the receiving one, off the chain if need be, arriving before or at the time of the transfer.
incorrect_answers: Into the USDC transaction's own on-chain data, where the customer's name sits beside the amount for anyone to read.
Nowhere: the rule covers bank wire transfers only, so a crypto transfer between two exchanges carries no data.
To a central FinCEN registry, which both exchanges must check before the USDC transfer can be released on chain.
questions.explanation: For $3,000 or more, the sending institution must pass on information about the sender and recipient. A crypto transfer counts, and the data need not travel in the same system as the value: it must arrive before or at the time of the transfer.

questions.question_stem: A trace leads into a permissioned ledger run by a bank consortium. The investigating agency is not a member. What can it read on that ledger?
questions.correct_answer: Nothing: there is no public node or explorer, so the records sit with the operator and its members.
incorrect_answers: Every transaction: each permissioned ledger keeps a public copy so that outsiders can check its records.
Only the hashes: outsiders get a hash of each transaction, while members read the full details.
Only the member names: the ledger publishes who belongs, while the transactions stay private.
questions.explanation: An outsider sees nothing: no public node, no explorer, no copy of the ledger. An on-chain trace stops at the operator's edge; the records are real, but they sit with the operator and its members.
